passage:
School counsellor's note, family meeting, 7 March.
Amandeep, fifteen, and her mother, Charu, came in after a big fight last week about a missed tuition class. Each told me what was said. Amandeep: "She said I'm useless and I'll never amount to anything." Charu: "I said you were being careless, and that I was worried." Both were completely certain, and both were close to tears. I didn't try to decide who was right; nobody had recorded it. I explained that our memory of a heated moment gets reshaped by what we feel and by what we think about it afterwards. Then I asked each of them what they had felt in that moment. Amandeep: "Small." Charu: "Scared for her." They looked at each other for a long time. We'll meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: What was the fight about?
qa.a: A missed tuition class.

qa.q: Why is Amandeep so sure her mother called her useless?
qa.a: Amandeep felt small and hurt in the moment, and that feeling shaped the memory, so 'careless' may have been remembered as 'useless'.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor ask about feelings instead of deciding who was right?
qa.a: With no record, the exact words can't be settled, but sharing what they felt, small and scared, helps them understand each other.

qa.q: How does Charu remember the argument?
qa.a: Charu remembers saying Amandeep was being careless and that she was worried, and feels scared for her daughter.

grounding: Shows a teenager and a parent each certain of different words in an argument, with memories shaped by feelings.

passage:
Sunday night
Big fight with Pa. Two weeks ago, when I asked about the school trip to Sikkim, he said, "Yes, you can go." I KNOW he did. I remember exactly: he was reading the paper and he said yes. Today he says he said, "We'll see, if your marks are okay." I said he's changing the story. He said I'm hearing what I want to hear.
I asked Siddharth, who was there. He said he honestly doesn't remember the exact words, only that Pa was busy with the paper.
Now I'm lying here wondering. I was so excited that day. Maybe I heard 'we'll see' and my brain turned it into yes. Maybe Pa said yes and forgot. I don't know any more. Tomorrow I'll ask Pa if we can start again from now, instead of arguing about then.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where was the school trip going?
qa.a: To Sikkim.

qa.q: Why is Tenzin now unsure about what Pa said?
qa.a: Tenzin feels confused and doubtful, realising the excitement that day might have turned 'we'll see' into 'yes' in memory.

qa.q: What does Tenzin plan to do tomorrow, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ask Pa to start again from now instead of arguing about the exact words, since neither memory can be proven.

qa.q: How does Pa remember the conversation?
qa.a: Pa remembers saying 'We'll see, if your marks are okay', and thinks Tenzin heard what Tenzin wanted to hear.

grounding: Shows a teenager and a parent each sure of different words, with the teen noticing how feelings might have shaped the memory.

passage: Vidya was certain. "The train is at 6:40, Francis. I booked it myself." She was so sure that they stopped for chai at the station entrance, even though the queue was long and the platform was at the far end. Francis frowned. "I thought you said ten past six?" "No. Forty. I remember typing it." At 6:02 Francis, uneasy, scrolled back through their chat and found the screenshot Vidya had sent the week before: Chennai train, 18:10. He held it up. Vidya stared at her own message. She could still see 6:40 in her head, clear as anything. "Run," she said. They made it with forty seconds to spare, bags bumping, chai left on the counter. On the train, breathing hard, Vidya said, "I was so sure." "I know," said Francis. "Sure isn't the same as right."

How did Vidya feel when she saw her own screenshot?
qa.a: Vidya felt shocked and embarrassed, because she could still clearly 'see' 6:40 in her head even though the message said otherwise.

qa.q: What could Vidya do the next time she feels certain about a detail like this?
qa.a: Check the ticket or message before acting on it, because feeling sure doesn't mean the memory is correct.

passage: At the family gathering in Satara, the talk turned, as always, to the great flood. Kamal said it was the year he started school, when the water reached the temple steps. Madhuri remembered it differently: she was sure she'd been in Class 3, and that the water had only reached the peepal tree. The cousins took sides. Madhuri felt the old urge to prove him wrong. Instead she said, "That's how I remember it, but I might be mixing it up." Later she looked in Aaji's tin trunk and found the panchayat's relief receipt, dated 2006. That made Kamal right about the year. The height of the water, nobody could check. At dinner she told him, smiling, "You win the year. Let's both keep our own water level."

qa.q: Which part of Madhuri's approach kept the peace?
qa.a: Checking a record for what could be checked, the year, and letting both memories stand for what couldn't, the water level.

Zanele was certain it was the university library, reaching for the same book. Abebe was just as sure it was the bus stop outside, in the rain. He felt the familiar itch to win. Then he remembered what his grandmother used to say: memories are soft clay. "I remember it as the bus stop," he said. "But let me check." He scrolled back through his oldest messages. The first one from Zanele said: 'Thanks for sharing your umbrella. Sorry I stole your book earlier!' Both were true, on the same afternoon. Zanele laughed. "So we were each remembering half." Abebe raised his glass. "To both halves."

Hostel warden's note, girls' block, 18 August.
On Sunday night, Sarita said she saw a white shape on the terrace. By Monday, six girls had seen it, and by Tuesday Tenzin was telling me in detail how the shape floated past her window and whispered her name. When I asked where she was at the time, she said she was in bed, asleep, until the others woke her. Her room faces the courtyard, not the terrace. I don't think she is lying; she was upset and sure. Group stories at night grow quickly, and she had heard this one told many times at dinner. I showed the girls the white bedsheet that had blown off the terrace line, and we talked about how shared stories can feel like our own memories. passage:
Note after Sunday lunch. Jagdish.
Rashmi is twenty now, home from college, and at lunch she told a story I had never heard: the day she was five and got lost at the Dussehra fair, and a policeman carried her on his shoulders to the loudspeaker stall. She described his moustache, the red lights, the smell of jalebis. She was close to tears telling it. Her mother and I looked at each other. It never happened. We never took her to that fair; she had chickenpox that year. But I didn't laugh. I told her gently that we had no memory of it, and asked where she thought it came from. She went quiet, then said her cousin used to tell a story just like that about himself. We sat together for a while. It clearly felt real to her, and that part matters.

qa.q: Why could Rashmi not have been at the fair that year?
qa.a: She had chickenpox that year.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi close to tears telling the story?
qa.a: Rashmi felt moved and frightened recalling it, because the scene was vivid and emotional, even though it never happened to her.

qa.q: How did Jagdish respond, and why was it kind?
qa.a: Jagdish didn't laugh, gently told Rashmi that the family had no memory of it, and asked where it might have come from, respecting that it felt real.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's mother react at lunch?
qa.a: Her mother exchanged a look with Jagdish, knowing it never happened, and joined in handling it gently.

passage:
Thursday night
Had the strangest conversation with Chinmay today. I was telling my roommate about the time I fell out of Ajoba's mango tree when I was eight and broke my arm. I remember everything: the rough bark, the snap, the smell of the hospital, the pink cast everyone signed. Chinmay, visiting, laughed. "Deepu, that was me. I broke my arm. You were the one who ran for help." I told him no way. He sent me a photo from Aai's album: Chinmay, eight, with a white cast, and me beside him, holding his hand.
I've been staring at the photo all night. The pink cast I remember doesn't exist. The feeling of falling feels completely real. How can a memory this vivid be wrong?
Deepika

qa.q: What colour was the cast in the photo?
qa.a: White.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel staring at the photo all night?
qa.a: Deepika feels shaken and confused, because the memory of falling feels completely real even though the photo shows it happened to Chinmay.

qa.q: What could Deepika take from this about vivid memories?
qa.a: That vividness and emotion don't prove a memory is accurate, so checking photos or asking family is wise before being certain.

qa.q: How did Chinmay react to Deepika's version?
qa.a: Chinmay laughed, then sent the photo to show it was his arm that broke and that Deepika ran for help.

passage: Felix saw the collision from a café window in Berlin: a cyclist and a delivery van at the corner. The cyclist was shaken but unhurt. qa.a: It recorded his memory soon after the event, before conversations could reshape it.

qa.a: Amara felt scared and upset, because she cycles through that corner every day.
